question: Autokinesis is the illusion in which:

options.text: A single, stationary point of light viewed against a dark, featureless background appears to move, even though it has not
A genuinely moving light appears stationary
Only occurs in bright daylight with a clear horizon
Is caused by a fault in the light itself rather than by the observer's visual system

explanation: Without a reference frame around it, a fixed point of light stared at for some time (such as a star, or a distant stationary light at night) can appear to drift or move, purely because the eye has nothing stable nearby to judge it against.

question: A pilot who mistakes an autokinetic illusion of a distant light for another aircraft's actual movement is at risk of:

options.text: Making an unnecessary avoidance manoeuvre, or misjudging a genuine traffic conflict because the false movement masks real cues
No practical consequence, since the illusion is purely visual and never affects decisions
Automatically correcting the illusion within less than a second
Experiencing the illusion only during daylight

explanation: Because autokinesis can suggest apparent movement that is not real, it can prompt unnecessary control inputs or confuse genuine traffic assessment at night — a reason to scan actively rather than fixate on a single distant light.

question: A "false horizon" illusion can occur when a pilot mistakes which of the following for the true horizon?

options.text: A sloping cloud deck, a line of coastal lights, or a line of terrain lit at an angle to the true horizontal
The attitude indicator itself
Only another aircraft's navigation lights
The aircraft's own wingtip lights

explanation: The brain readily accepts a strong, linear visual cue as "the horizon" even when it is sloped relative to true level — a sloping cloud bank or an angled line of ground lights can convincingly mimic the horizon and lead a pilot to roll the aircraft to match it, inducing an actual bank.

question: A "black-hole approach" refers to a night approach over dark, featureless terrain (such as water or unlit countryside) toward a lit runway, which characteristically causes a pilot to:

options.text: Perceive themselves as higher than they actually are, and so fly a dangerously low approach
Perceive themselves as lower than they actually are, and fly an excessively high approach
Have no distorted perception at all, since only the runway lights matter
Only occur during daylight approaches

explanation: With no lit terrain between the aircraft and the runway to provide normal depth and height cues, the brain tends to underestimate how low the aircraft actually is relative to the runway, tempting a pilot to fly a lower-than-intended approach — a pattern implicated in a number of controlled-flight-into-terrain accidents on approach.

question: The standard defence against a black-hole approach is to:

options.text: Rely on instrument guidance (such as a glideslope or VASI/PAPI) rather than the visual impression of height alone
Fly purely by the visual picture, trusting it more than any instrument guidance available
Approach at night only when there is no instrument guidance available
Increase speed significantly to compensate

explanation: Because the visual cues in a black-hole scenario are actively misleading, an objective vertical guidance reference — an ILS glideslope, a visual approach slope indicator, or a stabilised approach procedure — gives a true picture that the eye alone cannot be trusted to provide.

question: On approach to a runway that is narrower than the pilot is used to, the typical illusion produced is that the aircraft:

options.text: Appears to be higher than it actually is, tempting the pilot to fly a lower-than-normal approach
Appears to be lower than it actually is, tempting the pilot to fly a higher-than-normal approach
Has no effect on perceived height at all
Only matters for the landing flare, not the approach

explanation: A narrower-than-expected runway produces a visual picture similar to that of a normal-width runway seen from farther away, which the brain tends to interpret as being higher than the aircraft actually is — a bias toward flying the approach too low.

question: On approach to a runway that is wider than usual, the typical illusion produced is that the aircraft:

options.text: Appears to be lower than it actually is, tempting the pilot to fly a higher-than-normal approach, or to flare too high
Appears to be higher than it actually is, tempting the pilot to fly too low
Produces an identical effect to a narrower-than-normal runway
Has no bearing on the landing flare

explanation: A wider-than-expected runway visually resembles a normal-width runway seen from closer than it actually is, biasing perceived height downward — tempting the pilot to fly high on approach, or to round out and flare earlier than the actual height warrants.

question: An upsloping runway (one that rises away from the approach end) tends to create the illusion that the aircraft is:

options.text: Higher than it actually is, which can lead a pilot to fly a lower-than-normal approach
Lower than it actually is, leading to a higher-than-normal approach
Unaffected by runway slope in any way
Only relevant to the takeoff roll, never to landing

explanation: An upsloping runway's visual profile resembles that of a level runway seen from a greater height, biasing the pilot toward perceiving the aircraft as higher than it actually is and flying a correspondingly lower approach.

question: A downsloping runway tends to create the opposite illusion from an upsloping one, leading a pilot to:

options.text: Perceive the aircraft as lower than it actually is, tempting a higher-than-normal approach
Perceive the aircraft as higher than it actually is
Experience exactly the same illusion as with an upsloping runway
Experience no illusion, since slope only matters for upsloping runways

explanation: A downsloping runway's visual profile resembles that of a level runway seen from a lower height than the aircraft is actually at, biasing the pilot toward perceiving the aircraft as too low and correcting with a higher approach than is actually needed.

question: Flying an approach over featureless terrain such as water, snow or flat, unbroken desert is hazardous mainly because:

options.text: The lack of texture and reference points removes many of the normal visual cues used to judge height and closure rate above the surface
Featureless terrain always appears closer than it actually is, with no other effect
It has no effect on height judgement, only on heading judgement
It only matters at night, never in daylight

explanation: Normal height and closure judgement depends heavily on texture in the terrain below — trees, buildings, waves, snow drifts. A smooth, featureless surface removes those cues, which is why flat water, snow and smooth desert terrain are all specifically flagged as height-judgement hazards.

question: Rain streaking across a windscreen is well documented to cause which visual illusion?

options.text: Objects viewed through the rain-affected windscreen appear farther away and higher than they actually are
Objects appear closer and lower than they actually are
Rain on the windscreen has no effect on the perceived position of outside objects
Rain only affects colour perception, not distance

explanation: The way light refracts through rain streaks and droplets on the windscreen tends to make outside objects, including the runway, appear more distant and higher than they truly are, which has been linked to pilots flying lower-than-intended approaches in heavy rain.

question: Patchy fog or haze that reduces visibility along the approach path, without removing it entirely, can lead a pilot to:

options.text: Underestimate how far away the runway actually is, and fly an approach that is too low or too steep
Always overestimate distance and fly an excessively shallow approach
See no distortion of distance whatsoever, since fog only affects visibility range, not perceived distance
Experience the effect equally regardless of fog density

explanation: Reduced contrast and visual range through haze or fog tend to make the runway appear farther away than it truly is, which can prompt a pilot to descend or close the distance more aggressively than is actually appropriate, risking a low or unstable approach.

question: A pilot formation-flying or passing close to a large aircraft that is itself climbing or descending may experience the illusion that:

options.text: Their own aircraft is moving in the opposite sense to the other aircraft's actual motion, because the brain tends to interpret the nearer, larger object as the stable reference
Neither aircraft appears to be moving at all
Only the other aircraft can ever appear to move; one's own aircraft is always perceived correctly
The illusion only occurs when both aircraft are stationary on the ground

explanation: The visual system often treats a large, close object as the fixed frame of reference, so if that aircraft is actually climbing, a pilot can momentarily perceive their own aircraft as descending relative to it, even though it is their own aircraft that is actually holding a steady flight path.

question: "Flicker vertigo" refers to disorientation, nausea or even seizure-like symptoms in susceptible individuals, triggered by:

options.text: A light source flickering at a certain frequency, such as sunlight strobing through a rotating propeller disc, or a strobe light reflecting off cloud
A completely steady, non-flickering light source
Sound frequency alone, with no visual component
Only occurring in daylight with no artificial lighting involved

explanation: Certain flicker frequencies can provoke a disproportionate neurological response in susceptible individuals, ranging from mild disorientation and nausea to, rarely, seizures — which is why flashing anti-collision lights reflecting back off cloud at night are a recognised, specific hazard worth being aware of.

question: A practical response, if flicker vertigo symptoms are suspected during flight in cloud at night with a strobe light reflecting back, is to:

options.text: Turn off the strobe (leaving other required lighting on) to remove the specific flickering stimulus causing the problem
Increase the strobe's flash rate to resolve the issue
Stare directly at the strobe to let the eyes adjust
Continue unchanged, since the effect always resolves on its own within seconds

explanation: Removing the specific flickering stimulus — in this case, the strobe reflecting repeatedly off surrounding cloud — is the direct and practical fix, which is why many aircraft checklists call for anti-collision strobes to be switched off in instrument conditions where this reflection effect becomes a problem.

question: "Spatial disorientation", as a general term, describes a pilot's:

options.text: Incorrect perception of the aircraft's position, attitude or motion relative to the Earth
Correct perception of attitude, combined with a navigation error
A condition that can only occur while on the ground
A permanent, irreversible medical condition

explanation: Spatial disorientation is an umbrella term covering the whole family of illusions in this subject — somatogyral, somatogravic, visual illusions and others — all of which share the same core problem: the pilot's perceived attitude or motion does not match reality.

question: Spatial disorientation illusions are most likely to develop strongly when a pilot:

options.text: Has no clear, reliable outside visual reference, as in cloud, haze, darkness or featureless terrain
Has a sharp, unmistakable horizon clearly visible at all times
Is flying with full outside visibility over familiar, well-lit terrain
Is on the ground with the aircraft stationary

explanation: Nearly every illusion in this topic depends on the absence or ambiguity of a reliable outside reference — cloud, darkness, haze and featureless terrain all remove the clear visual information that would otherwise override a false vestibular or perceptual signal.

question: The single most consistent protective measure taught against spatial disorientation, across all its different forms, is to:

options.text: Trust and fly the flight instruments whenever bodily sensation and outside visual cues are unreliable or contradictory
Close the eyes briefly to let the vestibular system reset
Make control inputs based on physical sensation rather than instrument indications
Rely on a passenger's verbal description of the attitude

explanation: Every illusion in this topic works by fooling the senses or perception, not the instruments. The consistent defence across all of them is the same: when sensation and instruments disagree, trust the instruments, which is the entire basis of instrument flight training.

question: A city's lights seen beyond the runway during a night approach, mixed in with the runway and approach lighting, can contribute to disorientation mainly by:

options.text: Making it harder to distinguish the actual runway lighting pattern from background lights, increasing the risk of lining up on, or judging height against, the wrong reference
Having no effect whatsoever on a pilot's ability to judge the approach
Only being a problem during takeoff, never during landing
Always making the approach easier by providing more light overall

explanation: A cluttered night scene with city lights, roads and other lighting near the airport can make it genuinely harder to pick out the runway's own lighting pattern cleanly, increasing the chance of misjudging alignment or height against the wrong set of lights.

question: During the landing flare, correctly judging the aircraft's height above the runway depends heavily on:

options.text: Peripheral vision picking up the rate of apparent motion of the runway surface passing beneath and ahead of the aircraft
Central vision alone, focused directly on the far end of the runway
Hearing alone, with no visual component
The vestibular system exclusively, with no contribution from vision

explanation: Peripheral visual flow — the blur of apparent motion in the near ground as the aircraft descends — is a major contributor to judging closing height during the flare, which is part of why conditions that degrade this cue (darkness, fog, featureless terrain) make the flare noticeably harder to judge well.

question: A missed approach flown in low visibility, with a sudden application of climb power, is a scenario specifically associated with:

options.text: A somatogravic illusion, in which the forward acceleration from the thrust increase is misread as an excessive nose-up pitch
Autokinesis, since the runway lights have just gone out of view
A problem that can only occur in daylight
No illusion at all, since missed approaches are flown entirely on instruments by definition

explanation: A missed approach combines strong forward acceleration with the loss of outside visual reference — exactly the ingredients for a somatogravic illusion, and exactly why instrument reference during the pitch-up and power application of a missed approach matters as much as it does.

question: Briefing the likely illusions of a specific approach in advance (for example, "black-hole approach expected, watch the glideslope") is a useful defence mainly because:

options.text: Knowing an illusion is likely helps a pilot deliberately favour the instrument reference over the misleading visual impression when it actually occurs
Briefing an illusion in advance always prevents it from being experienced at all
Illusions can only affect a pilot who has not been briefed about them
This kind of briefing has no measurable safety value

explanation: Anticipating a specific illusion does not stop the sensory system from generating the false impression, but it does prime the pilot to recognise it for what it is and to lean more deliberately on instrument guidance rather than being caught by surprise.
